Verified against the on-disk PL 114 scan, archive.org patrologiaecurs06saingoog (raw/scans/pl114/), PDF page = (column + 11) / 2, RE-CALIBRATED before the read against the printed corner numbers: p. 223 = cols 435/436. Rendered at 200 dpi, full page width, and the whole line read at each site. — 2026-08-26: extended to p. 236 (cols 461/462) for the predicted 0462B site, corner numbers re-read before the crop, rendered at 600 dpi.
class: THREE DEFECTS IN ONE LINE, of two classes, all found while answering a question about a fourth thing. The translating agent flagged a full stop followed by a lower-case word at 0435B — declining to capitalize, because that would silently repair the plate's typography, and saying plainly it would read to a viewer as our own build defect. It was right to flag and right not to touch it. The plate answers: Migne prints a COLON there, and a colon before a lower-case word is ordinary. So the sentence was never his defect; the mark is ours. Reading the same line for that answer then produced two more — a second colon corrupted to a spaced hyphen, and a NORMALIZATION: Migne prints 'Chistus', missing its r, and the digitization tidied it to 'Christus'. That is addendum C exactly — the normalization class lives in the neighbours of the word you came to read, and nobody can flag it from the file, because a normalized form reads perfectly. The class now stands at six.

patches.why: The plate prints 'exterminantur : utramque'. Our text turned his colon into a full stop, which left a sentence apparently beginning in lower case — the thing the translator flagged. Restoring the colon removes the apparent defect without repairing anything of Migne's, and the English, which mirrored the oddity faithfully, becomes ordinary alongside it. ⚠ NOTE ON THE FIND STRING: the TEI breaks the line between 'exterminantur.' and 'utramque', so the patch must carry the newline. The first version of this patch was written against the CHUNKED text and matched zero times; chunk-work.mjs refused to run rather than proceed, which is the behaviour that check exists for.

patches.find:
Semen
Abrahae Christus est - in fide cujus
patches.replace:
Semen
Abrahae Chistus est : in fide cujus
patches.why: TWO corruptions in six words, and they must be repaired together. (1) The same colon-loss as above, here become a spaced hyphen — a mark Migne does not use anywhere in this book. (2) THE NORMALIZATION: the plate prints 'Chistus', without the r, and our source silently corrected it to 'Christus'. Our Latin column was therefore printing a word Migne did not print, in a line where he made a visible slip. Restoring it puts the defect back where the reader can see it; the English says Christ, as it must, and now carries a [sic:] because the plate licenses one — a marker asserts a defect and only a plate can license it. ⚠ The TEI breaks the line between 'Semen' and 'Abrahae', so this find string carries the newline too.

patches.find: fidei quam habebant fuit. ita et hoc lavacrum
patches.replace: fidei quam habebant fuit : ita et hoc lavacrum
patches.why: THE FOURTH STINT'S PREDICTION, READ AND CONFIRMED (2026-08-26). It flagged this as a second instance of the 0435B class -- a full stop before a lower-case word at a 'sicut ... ita' hinge, which is exactly where a colon belongs -- wrote the patch text, and did not patch. The plate settles it: PL 114 p. 236 (cols 461/462, corner numbers re-read before the crop) prints 'fidei quam habebant fuit : ita et hoc lavacrum'. A COLON. So this sentence, like 0435B, was never Migne's defect; the mark is ours, and the English's apparent mid-sentence full stop before a lower-case 'so' goes with it. Restoring the colon repairs nothing of Migne's. NOTE: unlike the two 0435B patches, the TEI does NOT break this line, so the find string carries no newline.

refuted.candidate: the lower-case word after a full stop
refuted.verdict: NOT a defect of Migne's and NOT ours to capitalize — his mark is a colon. Recorded so the question is not reopened: the translator's decision to mirror rather than repair was correct, and the repair belongs at the punctuation, not the capital.
